stem: Several months after an axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer, a client reports that the affected-side arm feels newly heavy and tight and appears mildly swollen. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Assess the affected arm, compare it with the other arm, and promptly arrange further evaluation because new heaviness, tightness, and swelling can indicate lymphedema.
options.B: Document the symptoms and reassess them at the next routine visit, because mild swelling after lymph-node surgery is expected unless it becomes functionally limiting.
options.C: Recommend an over-the-counter compression sleeve immediately and have the client choose a snug fit based on comfort until a formal evaluation can be scheduled.
options.D: Begin a vigorous resistance-exercise program with the affected arm to improve lymph flow, then arrange evaluation if the heaviness and swelling persist.

rationale: The National Cancer Institute states that removal of underarm lymph nodes during breast-cancer treatment increases lymphedema risk and advises clients to contact the health care team as soon as heaviness, tightness, swelling, or other early changes appear because earlier treatment is easier to control. NCI describes diagnosis as examination of the swollen area with comparison of the affected limb to the opposite limb and further testing when needed. Therefore A is correct. B delays evaluation of recognized early symptoms. C starts compression without the fitting and instruction NCI recommends from a nurse or certified lymphedema therapist. D uses an unsupervised vigorous program before assessment, whereas NCI advises developing a safe exercise program with the health care team.
educational_objective: After axillary lymph-node surgery, recognize new arm heaviness, tightness, or swelling as possible early lymphedema and obtain prompt assessment, including comparison with the opposite limb, before initiating compression or exercise treatment.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Lymphedema and Cancer; Lymphedema (PDQ®) — Health Professional Version
source_version_date: Lymphedema and Cancer updated March 6, 2024; Health Professional PDQ updated December 18, 2024; current pages accessed 2026-08-25
source_locator: Lymphedema and Cancer > What is lymphedema?: contact the doctor as soon as heaviness, swelling, or other signs appear because lymphedema is easier to control when treatment starts early. > What causes lymphedema? > Lymphedema and breast cancer: underarm lymph-node removal increases risk of lymphedema in the ipsilateral hand, arm, or chest. > What are symptoms of lymphedema?: slight changes, heavy/full/tight feeling, and swelling should be reported. > How is lymphedema diagnosed?: examine the swollen area and compare an affected arm or leg with the opposite limb; additional testing may identify other causes. > How is lymphedema treated? > Compression garments: a nurse or certified lymphedema therapist helps find garments that fit properly and teaches use. > Can I prevent lymphedema? > Exercise: discuss a safe exercise program with the doctor.
source_claim_supported: Axillary lymph-node removal raises lymphedema risk; new heaviness, tightness, or swelling should be reported and evaluated promptly, with affected-versus-unaffected limb comparison as part of assessment and clinician-guided compression/exercise management.

supporting_sources.organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
supporting_sources.locator: Diagnosis of Lymphedema > Signs, Symptoms, and Physical Examination: unilateral edema in a client with risk factors such as prior axillary dissection should prompt clinical evaluation and differential diagnosis. > Diagnostic Testing > Limb measurements: compare affected and unaffected arms. > Nonsurgical Options > Compression garments and Physical exercise: compression and exercise are therapeutic interventions that require appropriate selection and individualized use.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Post-axillary-dissection arm swelling warrants clinical assessment rather than assumption or unsupervised treatment.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p. 42 (PDF p. 45): perform focused assessments; recognize trends and changes in client condition and intervene as needed; evaluate client responses to procedures and treatments; use precautions to prevent injury and/or complications associated with a procedure or diagnosis.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — recognition and assessment of possible treatment-related upper-extremity lymphedema
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four actions to remove the absolute-word cue and make the alternatives clinically plausible. The corrected distractors test delayed evaluation, unsupervised compression fitting, and vigorous exercise before assessment while preserving direct NCI support for early recognition and prompt evaluation.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Breast-cancer treatment complication — possible upper-extremity lymphedema
audit_findings.stem: PASS — identifies a clear risk factor and multiple early lymphedema symptoms while avoiding a confirmed diagnosis that would bypass assessment.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly follows NCI guidance to recognize early symptoms, examine the affected area, compare limbs, and obtain prompt evaluation; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — observation can be part of follow-up, but NCI advises prompt reporting/evaluation of even slight new heaviness, tightness, or swelling.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — compression can be therapeutic, but NCI recommends proper garment fitting and instruction rather than self-selection before evaluation.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — exercise may benefit lymph flow, but NCI advises a safe individualized program and new symptoms should be assessed before unsupervised vigorous resistance training.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only choice that prioritizes assessment and prompt evaluation without prematurely initiating treatment.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B delays recognized symptoms, C self-initiates compression without fitting/evaluation, and D self-initiates vigorous exercise before assessment.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all options are closely matched in length and specificity and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Reduction of Risk Potential directly includes focused assessment and recognition/intervention for changes related to treatments and procedures.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether compression or exercise could reasonably start immediately; NCI places evaluation and appropriate clinician/CLT guidance before individualized treatment, so A remains uniquely best for a new symptomatic presentation.
